title: From local leagues to the Premier Division: how club table tennis works in Britain
seo_title: How club table tennis works in Britain: leagues explained
description: How club table tennis in Britain fits together: local leagues, county leagues and the British Clubs League, with divisions, promotion and who can play.
summary: Most club players start in a local league on weekday evenings. The best teams can enter the British Clubs League, a national pyramid that runs from National C up to the Premier Division.
key_points: Local leagues are the base: weekday evening matches through the winter, with divisions, promotion and relegation run by each league.
Clubs, not players, enter teams, and the league registers each player.
The British Clubs League is Table Tennis England's national team competition, played over weekends at central venues, with senior, women's, veterans' and youth sections.
The senior British Clubs League is a pyramid: Premier Division, Championship, then National A, B and C divisions.
Local leagues need Compete membership; the British Clubs League needs Compete Plus.
body: Club table tennis in Britain works in layers. At the bottom are local leagues, where clubs enter teams that play on weekday evenings through the winter. Above them is the British Clubs League, Table Tennis England's national team competition, played over weekends at central venues and topped by the senior Premier Division. Each layer has its own divisions, with teams promoted and relegated at the end of every season.
## Local leagues: where almost everyone starts

Most competitive table tennis in England is played in local leagues. In 2024-25 Table Tennis England, the sport's governing body in England, had 139 local leagues affiliated, plus four regional and county leagues. Each league runs its own divisions, fixtures and rules within the national regulations.

Teams are normally two or three players. Matches are usually on weekday evenings at one team's club, with a winter season running from around late September to March. In the most common three-player format each player meets each of the three opponents, and many leagues add a doubles to make 10 individual matches. Our guide to [how team matches work](/guide/team-table-tennis-format.html) explains the scoring.

Bigger leagues have several divisions of around 10 to 14 teams, each playing the others home and away. Teams go up or down at the end of the season, often two at a time, and the league decides how many. You do not join a league as an individual: your club enters teams, and the league registers each player. Our guide to [finding a club and joining a league](/guide/find-a-table-tennis-club-england.html) explains the first steps.
## County and regional leagues

Between the local leagues and the national competition sit a handful of regional and county leagues, which draw stronger teams from a wider area. They are the exception rather than a fixed rung, and a club does not have to come through one to enter the British Clubs League. County associations also pick county teams for the national County Championships, which are separate from club play.
## The British Clubs League

The British Clubs League (BCL) is a competition for club teams from the British Isles. Since 2024-25 it has brought the old British League competitions under one name. Its regulations give it four sections: senior, women's, youth and veterans'. Regional cadet (under-15) and junior (under-19) leagues, once the National Cadet and Junior Leagues, are run alongside it.

Any club affiliated to Table Tennis England, or to the associations of Scotland, Wales, Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man, can enter, either through its local league or by affiliating directly. That is why the BCL is British rather than English. It costs more than a local league: in 2026-27 a senior team outside the top two divisions pays £827 to enter from a Premier Club, rising to £1,257 for a Premier Division team from a club that is only registered.

Instead of weekly fixtures, BCL teams travel to central venues and play several matches over a weekend. In 2026-27 the senior section has five weekends between September and April, the fourth of them for the Championship only, and the Premier Division has four weekends of its own. The women's, veterans' and youth sections each play over two weekends.
## The senior divisions

The senior section is a pyramid. At the top is the Premier Division, with a maximum of eight teams. Below it is the Championship, with up to 10, then two National A divisions, four National B divisions and up to eight National C divisions. No club can have more than one team in the same Premier, Championship, National A or National B division.

The formats change as you climb. Premier Division teams have four players, three of whom play singles and any two the doubles, for six singles and one doubles; a win is worth three points and a defeat in a completed match one point. The Championship plays eight singles and no doubles. The lower divisions play eight singles and a doubles. Every individual match is the best of five games.

To play in the Premier Division a player must be in the top 100 of the men's open rating list or the top 20 of the women's senior list, or near the top of the junior lists. In a Premier match-day squad a club can name only one player who is not affiliated to one of the home nations' associations.
## Women's, veterans' and youth sections

The women's and veterans' sections use teams of three playing six singles, with no doubles. Their divisions have five to eight teams. Veterans must be 40 or over on 31 December in the current membership year, and the veterans' section has men's open divisions and women's divisions. The youth section has its own Premier Division and lower divisions.

The cadet and junior leagues work differently. They are played on four days a season at about 15 regional hosts in England, and there is no promotion or relegation from one season to the next: the divisions are formed again each year.
## Promotion, relegation and new teams

In the senior BCL, the highest-placed eligible team in each division below the Championship goes up, and the two lowest-placed teams in the division above come down to make room. The Championship winner is promoted to the Premier Division, as long as its club does not already have a team there, and up to two Premier teams are relegated. In the women's and veterans' sections the top two in each division go up and the bottom two go down, except in the veterans' men's Division 1 groups, where only the winners are promoted.

Table Tennis England forms the divisions each summer. Relegated teams take the top places in the draw and promoted teams the lowest. In the lower senior tiers, teams are placed on a best fit by geography, depending on where the host venues are, so you may not be grouped with the nearest clubs. New teams join from a waiting list and start in the lowest tier, with teams from Premier and Associate clubs given priority in the women's, veterans' and youth sections.
## Who can play and what membership you need

For a local league you need Compete membership of Table Tennis England, which costs £26 for adults in 2026-27. The British Clubs League requires Compete Plus, at £49 for adults, or a visiting player's upgrade for those registered elsewhere. A player can be registered for only one club in each BCL section, and clubs must list their players in order of strength, so their best players cannot be hidden in lower teams.
## Your next steps

If you are new, start with a local league and look at [how ratings work for club players](/guide/table-tennis-england-ratings.html), since ratings decide where you can play in the BCL. Then follow this season's [British Clubs League](/clubs/british-league.html) tables, and read [how table tennis is run in England](/guide/table-tennis-england-explained.html) to see where the counties and the governing body fit.
